43.title: The sheet of flowers, 1539
43.hook: tradition says that when Nanak died, Hindus and Muslims both claimed his body, and under the sheet they found only flowers
43.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's passing, traditionally dated 1539 at Kartarpur, where Gurdwara Darbar Sahib keeps both a samadh and a grave; the story of the flowers is told as a sign that he belonged to all people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tests of Lehna, and wet grass on fine clothes. Your line was just do it well. Which task did you finish without a word of complaint? Day forty-three.

Think about the last funeral you went to. How much of it was about who the person was, and how much was about who gets to say goodbye, and how. Families argue at funerals. Communities do too. Kartarpur, 1539. Guru Nanak is about seventy years old, and he's dying. Word spreads through the villages, and people come. Hindus who had followed him, and Muslims who had followed him. And as they gather, a hard question rises. Hindus cremate their dead. Muslims bury theirs. So when the Guru is gone, which will it be? Who does he belong to? Today, how tradition says that question was answered.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SAY GOODBYE?` → `KARTARPUR, 1539.` → `HINDUS CREMATE. MUSLIMS BURY.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak heard the argument and settled it before it could start. Bring flowers, he said. Hindus, lay yours on my right side. Muslims, lay yours on my left. Whichever flowers are still fresh in the morning, that side may do as it wishes. Then he drew a sheet over himself, and died. In the morning his followers lifted the sheet. The body was gone. There were only the flowers, on both sides, and both were fresh. So, the story says, they cut the sheet in two. The Hindus cremated their half. The Muslims buried theirs. And at Kartarpur today, there is a memorial and a grave, side by side. Sikhs hear this story in different ways. For many it's a miracle, a last sign. For others it's a picture of what the whole life meant. Either way, look at the shape of it. Remember his first words after the river: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. He didn't say that to erase anyone. Both groups kept their own ways; both got to grieve as their tradition taught. What he refused was to be owned by one side against the other. Even at the very end, he gave both sides something. Flowers for everyone. That's where Guru Nanak's story closes, and with it twenty-two days of it: a boy at Talwandi, the river, the rebab, the road, Kartarpur. But he didn't leave the community without a leader. Before he died, he had already chosen who would carry the light, and given him a new name. That's tomorrow.
screen: `FLOWERS ON THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.` · `UNDER THE SHEET, ONLY FLOWERS.` · `THE SHEET CUT IN TWO.` · `NOT OWNED BY ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `FLOWERS FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: place a flower somewhere today. For now, settle and choose where. A desk at work. A grave you haven't visited. The doorstep of a neighbor you don't know well. A shared kitchen. If there's no flower handy, a leaf or a picture will do. Think of someone whose goodness belongs to more than one group of people, and let the flower be for them. The bell holds the time.
The sheet of flowers. Tradition's story of Guru Nanak's death: both communities' flowers fresh, and the sheet shared between them. Today's word.
Your line: flowers for everyone. Today, when two sides want the same thing, look for the answer that gives something to both. Day forty-three.

44.title: Lehna becomes Angad
44.hook: Nanak names Lehna his successor and calls him Angad, part of my own body
44.howItsDone: Sikhs understand the ten Gurus as one light passing through ten bodies, and they refer to the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib as angs, limbs of the Guru; Guru Angad's accession is remembered each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sheet of flowers, and the Guru who belonged to no one side. Your line was flowers for everyone. Where did you find an answer that gave something to both? Day forty-four.

When a founder steps down, everyone assumes they know who's next. The eldest son takes over the family shop. The deputy gets the corner office. Guru Nanak had two grown sons. The elder, Sri Chand, was a deeply devout man, an ascetic who had renounced ordinary life. The younger, Lakhmi Das, was a householder with a family. Either would have been the obvious choice. But for years Nanak had been watching someone else: the trader who'd carried the wet grass, cleared the ditch and fished the bowl out of dirty water. Today we step back a little in time, to a few months before the flowers, and the day Nanak made his choice.
screen: `EVERYONE ASSUMES THE SON.` → `TWO SONS, BOTH DEVOUT.` → `THE GURU WAS WATCHING SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Nanak placed a coconut and five copper coins before Lehna and bowed to him. The teacher bowed to the student. Then he gave him a new name: Angad. And that name is today's word, inside it. Ang means a limb, a part of the body. So Angad is often explained as part of my own body. The Guru was saying: this man isn't my replacement, he's me, continued. There's a line in the scripture, in a ballad sung by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, that says it plainly. The light was the same, the way was the same; the king had only changed his body. That's the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus. Not ten different teachers with ten different messages, but one light, passed from one body to the next, like a flame lit from a flame. Which is why each Guru, when he wrote hymns, signed them not with his own name but with Nanak's. And here's a detail Sikhs love. Ang also names the pages of the Sikh scripture. You don't say page 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib; you say Ang 360. Each page is a limb of the Guru. So the word that named the second Guru now names every page of the book the Sikhs call their Guru today. One more thing to notice: Nanak didn't choose by blood. He chose the one who had become a servant. The light went to the one who could carry it, and it's still traveling.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think who carries your work on. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you care about: a skill, a family recipe, a way of doing your job, a value your parents gave you. Who is going to carry it after you? A child, a colleague, a friend, a student. See their face. If nobody comes to mind, notice that too, and wonder who it might be. The bell holds the time.
Ang. A limb, a part of the body; inside the name Angad, and the word Sikhs use for every page of their scripture. Today's word.
Your line: passing the light. Today, teach one thing you know to someone who could carry it on. Day forty-four.

45.title: The Guru's script
45.hook: at Khadur, Guru Angad shapes and teaches the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people can read the hymns
45.howItsDone: Sikh children often learn Gurmukhi at home or in gurdwara classes so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves; any Sikh, of any gender or caste, may read from the scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang: a limb, and the name Angad, part of my own body. Your line was passing the light. What did you teach someone who could carry it on? Day forty-five.

Think about the first time you read something by yourself. A cereal box, a street sign, a picture book. Something clicked, and a whole world that had belonged to grown-ups suddenly belonged to you too. For most people in the Punjab of the 1500s, that click never came. Reading was for priests, scholars and clerks. Sacred texts were in Sanskrit or Arabic or Persian, languages ordinary farmers didn't speak, and in scripts they couldn't read. And Guru Nanak's hymns, sung in the people's own language, were being passed along by memory and in rough notes. The new Guru, Angad, moved to a village called Khadur, and there, tradition says, he sat down with the children. Today, the letters he taught.
screen: `THE FIRST TIME YOU READ ALONE.` → `READING WAS FOR THE FEW.` → `GURU ANGAD SITS WITH THE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The script is called Gurmukhi. Guru is the teacher, and mukh is the mouth, so Gurmukhi is often explained as from the mouth of the Guru. It's the alphabet the Sikh scripture is written in, and the one Punjabi is written in across India today. Now, it's worth being careful here. Guru Angad didn't invent writing out of nothing. Scripts much like it were already used in the Punjab, especially by traders keeping accounts. What Sikh tradition credits him with is shaping those letters into a clear, standard alphabet, putting them in order, and teaching them, so anyone could learn to read the Guru's words. Tradition says he taught the letters to children himself, and helped put together an early primer. Think about what that means. On many paths, the holy words sat in a language only specialists could read, so ordinary people needed someone in between. Guru Angad did the opposite. He put the hymns in the people's own language, in letters a farmer's child could learn, so the word could go straight from the page into anyone's life. That's a big part of why, to this day, Sikhs treat reading the scripture as something for everyone, man or woman, of any caste. There's no priestly class that holds the book. Anyone who can read Gurmukhi can read the Guru. And the first symbol you learned, Ik Onkar, the numeral one and its curve, is written in these letters.
screen: `GURMUKHI — FROM THE GURU'S MOUTH.` · `SHAPED, ORDERED AND TAUGHT.` · `THE PEOPLE'S OWN LANGUAGE.` · `NO ONE STANDS BETWEEN.` · then, large: `LETTERS FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your name slowly by hand. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Write your name, one letter at a time, slower than you ever do. Watch each shape form. Somebody taught you these letters once. Maybe you remember who. A parent at a kitchen table, a teacher in a classroom. Let your pen move slowly enough to remember them. The bell holds the time.
The Guru's script. Gurmukhi, the letters Guru Angad shaped and taught at Khadur so ordinary people could read the hymns. Today's word.
Your line: letters for everyone. Today, explain one thing you know in the plainest words you can, so anyone could understand it. Day forty-five.

46.title: Mata Khivi's kitchen
46.hook: Guru Angad's wife runs the langar and is remembered for serving rich rice pudding to all
46.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Mata Khivi as a shaper of the langar, the free kitchen found at every gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve anyone who comes, seated together; kheer is still often served there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru's script, Gurmukhi, shaped so anyone could read. Your line was letters for everyone. What did you explain in the plainest words you could? Day forty-six.

In a lot of families, the most important teaching doesn't happen in a classroom or a place of worship. It happens in the kitchen. Who gets fed first. Whether there's always room for one more. What you do when someone shows up hungry and unannounced. At Khadur, while Guru Angad was teaching the letters, there was another teacher at work, and her classroom was a kitchen. Her name was Mata Khivi. Mata means mother, a title of respect. She was Guru Angad's wife, and she ran the langar, the free community kitchen where everyone who came was fed, sitting side by side. Today, what she served, and what it taught.
screen: `THE KITCHEN TABLE TEACHES.` → `MATA KHIVI, GURU ANGAD'S WIFE.` → `SHE RAN THE LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Here's what's remarkable: Mata Khivi is in the scripture. In the Guru Granth Sahib, in a ballad by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, there's a line about her. It says, in paraphrase, that Khivi is a good woman who gives cool, leafy shade to everyone, like a great tree. And it says that in her kitchen the Guru's bounty is shared out, and the kheer, rice pudding rich with ghee, the clarified butter, tastes like nectar. Think about that. In a book of hymns about God, there's a line honoring a woman for her cooking and her kindness. That's not a small thing. It says the kitchen is holy ground too. Why rice pudding? Because in that time and place, kheer made with ghee was a rich food, the kind of thing served at celebrations, or to honored guests. In most places, the poor got coarse bread, if anything. Mata Khivi served the good stuff, to everyone, the laborer and the landlord at the same meal. Remember Lalo's bread? That was honest food earned by hard work. This is the other side of the same teaching: when you share, share the best you have. Sikh tradition remembers Mata Khivi as one of the people who made the langar what it is today, not just a charity meal but a table where everyone is an honored guest. Every gurdwara kitchen in the world, stirring a pot of dal for strangers tonight, is in some way still her kitchen.
screen: `MATA KHIVI IS IN THE SCRIPTURE.` · `SHADE LIKE A GREAT TREE.` · `KHEER WITH GHEE, FOR EVERYONE.` · `SHARE THE BEST YOU HAVE.` · then, large: `THE KITCHEN IS A TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone a sweet thing. Settle, and think who. A coworker, a neighbor, the person who delivers your mail, someone at home. Not the leftover cookie; the good one. Picture handing it over, and their face. If you can't give food, give something else sweet: a real compliment, a thank-you note. Then plan when you'll do it today. The bell holds the time.
Mata Khivi's kitchen. The langar at Khadur, where Guru Angad's wife served rich rice pudding to all, and is honored in the scripture for it. Today's word.
Your line: the kitchen is a teacher. Today, when you share food, share the best of it, not the rest of it. Day forty-six.

47.title: The wrestling ground
47.hook: Guru Angad encourages exercise and wrestling so body and spirit grow strong together
47.tomorrow: an old man hears a hymn
47.howItsDone: Sikh tradition values physical health and strength alongside prayer; many gurdwaras host sports, and martial arts such as gatka are practiced in Sikh communities, with Khadur Sahib's Mall Akhara remembered as Guru Angad's wrestling ground.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Khivi's kitchen, and rich rice pudding for everyone. Your line was the kitchen is a teacher. Who got the good one from you? Day forty-seven.

There's an old idea, in a lot of places, that the spiritual life happens from the neck up. The body is just the thing that carries your soul around, and maybe gets in the way. So holy people are pictured as thin, pale and still. Now picture Khadur in the 1540s. In the mornings, hymns. At midday, the kitchen, with Mata Khivi's pudding. And in the evenings, tradition says, a patch of packed earth where young men stripped to the waist and wrestled, while the Guru himself watched and cheered them on. Today, the word for that patch of earth.
screen: `SPIRITUAL FROM THE NECK UP?` → `KHADUR IN THE 1540S.` → `PACKED EARTH, AND WRESTLERS.`

segments.voice: It's called an akhara: a wrestling ground, a training place. Across South Asia, wrestling was an old and serious art, with its own teachers, its own discipline and its own pits of soft earth. Sikh tradition says Guru Angad set up an akhara at Khadur, and a gurdwara there is still named for it, the Mall Akhara, the wrestlers' ground. He encouraged young people to exercise, to wrestle, to be strong and healthy. Why would a Guru care about push-ups? Because on this path, the body isn't the enemy. Guru Nanak had told the yogis on the mountain that you don't need to leave the world to find God. You live in it, unstained. And living in the world takes a body that can work a field, carry water, stand up for a neighbor. Health isn't vanity; it's part of being useful. The wrestling picture shows up in the scripture, too. In a hymn by the fifth Guru, Arjan, the speaker describes himself as a wrestler, a champion of the Lord, who has come into the arena of the world. Life itself is the akhara, and the real opponents are things like ego, greed and anger. So the wrestling ground at Khadur was both things at once: a real place to train the body, and a picture of the struggle inside. Later Gurus would build on this. Within a century, Sikhs would need all the strength they had. But that story comes later. Today it's simply this: the body counts too.
screen: `AKHARA — A WRESTLING GROUND.` · `THE BODY ISN'T THE ENEMY.` · `STRONG ENOUGH TO BE USEFUL.` · `LIFE ITSELF IS THE ARENA.` · then, large: `THE BODY COUNTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move your body for three minutes. Stand up if you can. Roll your shoulders. Stretch your arms up, then fold forward. March in place, or do a few squats, or just walk around the room. If you can't stand, move what you can: hands, neck, breath. Don't make it a workout. Make it a thank-you to the body that carries you. The bell holds the time.
Akhara. A wrestling ground; at Khadur, a place where Guru Angad had young people train their bodies alongside their spirits. Today's word.
Your line: the body counts too. Today, take the stairs, or the long way, or a walk at lunch, and call it part of your practice. Day forty-seven.

48.title: An old man hears a hymn
48.word: An old man hears a hymn
48.hook: past sixty, Amar Das hears Guru Angad's daughter Bibi Amro singing Nanak's words at dawn, and goes to find the Guru
48.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das as the third Guru and tell of Bibi Amro's singing as the moment that brought him to Guru Angad; many Sikhs begin the day by reciting or listening to the Gurus' hymns before dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the akhara, the wrestling ground at Khadur. Your line was the body counts too. How did you move today? Day forty-eight.

Have you ever heard a song drift out of an open window and stopped walking? You didn't choose it. You weren't looking for it. It just found you. Here's a man who has been looking his whole life. His name is Amar Das. He's past sixty, a respected man in his village, and deeply devout. Tradition says he has walked to the Ganges on pilgrimage again and again, some say twenty times. He's done everything a devout man is supposed to do, and he still feels something missing. His nephew has married a young woman named Bibi Amro, who happens to be Guru Angad's daughter. And one morning before dawn, Amar Das hears her singing while she works. Today, the hymn that stopped him.
screen: `A SONG FROM AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `AMAR DAS, PAST SIXTY, STILL SEARCHING.` → `BIBI AMRO SINGS AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: She was singing a hymn of Guru Nanak's. Tradition doesn't agree on exactly which one, but the effect is the same in every telling. Amar Das stood still and listened, and then he asked her: whose words are those? My father's teacher, she said, Guru Nanak. And my father, Guru Angad, carries his light now, at Khadur. So an old man, a man of standing, got up and went to find a teacher about twenty-five years younger than himself. He bowed at Guru Angad's feet, and stayed. He would become the third Guru, and he wouldn't take up that role until his seventies. Notice a few things. First, who carried the hymn. Not a priest, not a scholar. A young woman singing while she did her morning work. The word traveled the way it was meant to, through ordinary people's voices, in their own language. That's what Guru Angad's letters and Mardana's rebab were for. Second, what the hymns are, on this path. Sikhs call the Gurus' words bani, and they treat bani itself as a teacher, as alive. A hymn heard at the right moment can change a whole life. And third, age. Amar Das had every reason to think his path was settled. He'd done the pilgrimages. He was old. Instead he started again as a beginner, and spent more than a decade learning to serve before anyone called him Guru. Sikhs tell his story to say that the door is open at any age, and it's never too late to hear something new.
screen: `WHOSE WORDS ARE THOSE?` · `AN OLD MAN BOWS TO A YOUNGER TEACHER.` · `BANI — THE WORD AS A LIVING TEACHER.` · `STARTING AGAIN AS A BEGINNER.` · then, large: `IT'S NEVER TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen closely to one song. Pick one now, any song, maybe one you haven't heard in years, or one someone you love used to sing. Close your eyes if you can. Listen to the words as if you're hearing them for the first time, like an old man stopped outside a window at dawn. Is there one line in it you never really heard before? The bell holds the time.
An old man hears a hymn. Amar Das, past sixty, stopped by Bibi Amro's dawn singing, who went to find Guru Angad and became the third Guru. Today's word.
screen: `AN OLD MAN HEARS A HYMN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it's never too late. Today, start one small thing you told yourself you were too old for. Day forty-eight.

49.title: The water carrier
49.hook: for years he carries water for Guru Angad before dawn; tradition says he stumbled by a weaver's peg and was mocked as homeless
49.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water as a model of seva, humble service; Guru Angad's reply to the weaver's wife is often recited in the story, and many Sikhs volunteer in small, unseen tasks at the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an old man hears a hymn, and Amar Das starts again as a beginner. Your line was it's never too late. What did you start? Day forty-nine, the end of a week.

Think of the people who do the same small job, faithfully, for years. The crossing guard who's there every morning in the rain. The neighbor who's brought in your trash cans since you moved in. The parent who packs the lunch every single school day. Nobody writes songs about them. Amar Das, the old man who'd come to Khadur, took on a job like that. Every morning, long before sunrise, he walked to the river Beas, filled a pitcher with water, and carried it back for Guru Angad's bath. It was a walk of several miles, there and back, in the dark, every day, in every season. Tradition says he did it for about twelve years. Today, one stormy night on that road.
screen: `THE SAME SMALL JOB, FOR YEARS.` → `TO THE RIVER AND BACK, BEFORE DAWN.` → `ABOUT TWELVE YEARS.`

segments.voice: It was dark and pouring rain, tradition says, and the old man was coming back with the full pitcher. Near a weaver's house he tripped over a peg in the ground, one of the stakes weavers use to stretch their thread, and fell. He didn't spill the water. But the noise woke the weaver, who asked who was out there at that hour. His wife answered, scornfully, that it must be Amru, the homeless one, who had no place of his own and hung around the Guru for scraps. Amar Das didn't argue. He picked himself up and carried the water home. When the story reached Guru Angad, tradition says, he answered with a list of honors: Amar Das is the home of the homeless, the honor of those with no honor, the strength of those with none. Not long after, he named Amar Das the third Guru. Why do Sikhs keep telling this? Because it turns the insult inside out. The one mocked as having no place becomes the one who gives everyone a place. And look back at the week. The sheet of flowers, for everyone. Lehna becomes Angad, part of the Guru's own body. The Guru's script, letters for everyone. Mata Khivi's kitchen. The wrestling ground. An old man who heard a hymn. And now a water carrier on a dark road. Almost every one of these people was chosen, or remembered, for faithfulness in things nobody was watching. Guru Angad's light passed to the man who carried the water.
screen: `A WEAVER'S PEG, IN THE RAIN.` · `AMRU, THE HOMELESS ONE.` · `THE HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · `THE WEEK: FAITHFUL, UNWATCHED.` · then, large: `FAITHFUL IN SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one humble job faithfully. Settle, and think of one small thing you do for someone that nobody notices. Filling the water jug. Taking out the recycling. Checking on an elderly neighbor. Picture doing it today, a little more carefully than usual, and without mentioning it to anyone. If someone mocks it, or ignores it, let it go. Just carry the water. The bell holds the time.
The water carrier. Amar Das, carrying water for Guru Angad for years before dawn, mocked as homeless, and named the home of the homeless. Today's word.
Your line: faithful in small things. Today, thank one person whose small, faithful job makes your day work. Day forty-nine.

fork.setup: you're an old man who's just fallen in the mud in the dark, and a stranger calls you a homeless hanger-on. what do you do?
options: argue and explain who you are.
pick yourself up and carry the water home.
give up the job; it's not worth it.
fork.reveal: Amar Das said nothing and carried the water home. Guru Angad called him the home of the homeless, and soon named him Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service; the heart of the water carrier's years.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man did a chore.
what it means: faithfulness in small, unseen work, and an insult turned inside out.
what a scholar hears: Amar Das became Guru in 1552; the weaver story is tradition, and the Goindval he later built grew up near that same river road.
